blocks.x: Okay, give me a name, please. My name is Lee Cowell.
When were you born and where? I was born on October 11, 1938, in New Orleans.
Have you lived in New Orleans all your life?
No, I lived in Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, about 60 miles in New Orleans. Seven years. From what age to what age? From the age of 10 to the age of 16.
When did you first become aware of the existence of such a form of music as New Orleans jazz?
Well, when I was about 12 years old, I heard for the first time Pop Selstein's band. And I believe it was the old Pestridge-Chan Yacht Club.
What did you think of the music?

Oh, I thought it was very good. I enjoyed it thoroughly. What about your friends? They all liked it, too. As a matter of fact, we used to make a point of going to all the dances that they had. To hear Pop Selstein.
What about your parents and your parents' friends? Do you know what they thought of it?

Well, my parents, of course, had heard Dixieland ever since it first began back in the early 20s and everything. And they, I'd say they liked Dixieland. But I mean, they wouldn't go out of their way to hear it.

But you would go out of their way to hear it. And you said your friends liked it, too? Yes, they all liked it. But would you think of it just something to music that you enjoyed listening to, to dance to, or do you think of it as an art form?

Well, of course, for us, it was the only kind of music we would listen to. I don't know. At that age, I don't believe we ever really considered things as art forms. But that was all we wanted to listen to, certainly.
And you say you first started listening to it in about 1950, you would say? Yes, 50 or 51. And your group liked it. Did they ever continue to like it, would you say?
Well, I myself liked Dixieland well enough. I thought I'd progress some progressive music more. And a lot of my friends have switched to liking what they call rock and roll them.
Well, could you say about when they, stop liking New Orleans jazz design, liking rock and roll?
I'd say when rock and roll or rhythm and blues, it used to be, first came out about five years ago, in 1953.
Well, they, when they did like it from 51 to 53, did they prefer jazz or popular music?
Oh, yeah, of course.
Do you know that many people now who really like jazz?

Dixieland? Yeah. Yeah, I know quite a few people who like Dixieland. When I say they like rock and roll, I don't mean they have totally given up Dixieland or anything like that. They just prefer the, say like, as if there were two dancers in a night, and one of them had a rock and roll band, and the other had, say, Selstein. Well, I think most of them go to the dance that had the rock and roll band. But if there was one, if there was a dance with Selstein, they wouldn't have loved it.

We'd say that the attitude, most of the people that listen to New Orleans jazz now is, that it's just something to dance to, and have a good, accompany a good time, or what they think of it as great music. And I think some people think of classical music as great music.

I think some people think of, uh, Dixieland, and when you say Dixieland, I take it, you mean the, uh, New Orleans music. New Orleans jazz. I think some of them would, would listen to it as an odd poem, which is, I believe, would you, but, uh, I think the majority of them would just listen to it as good time music, just in more or less the same spirit as they'd listen to the rhythm and blues.

Do you think, anything else to add on the subject of social accessibility of blues jazz? Oh, uh, what, you said, at dance, would you say that, for the majority of social functions, from, say, 1950 to 1953, that would have, uh, New Orleans jazz bands, if they could do it? Oh,

certainly. Everybody trying to get Celestein. He was, uh, he prayed to man. They haven't got anybody else? Or was it just Celestein? Not that I know of. They didn't have Celestein, they just had, uh, a Pops band, which nobody could stand. And,
would you say, who said, nowadays, they tend to hire, like, an old band's rather?
Yes. How do some people still do their Celestein for calling? Yes. Um,
what about the debutant parties? I mean, high, high, high social functions. What, what, would you say, what have you noticed, mostly?
Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Hmm. Well, I think they tend to, uh, get, people on Celestein, if they intend to have that kind of music.

But, would they, would you say, that they have more, of, uh, uh, the Warriors Jazz, or, and then, uh, uh, uh, sweet band, or, you know, a big band playing popular music? Would you think they tend to get more?
Yeah, I think they probably tend to get more pop music.
Think of anything else you can add, son? No.
No, not really. Um, thank you very much. Thank you.

segments.title: Name, birth in 1938 and years in Bay St. Louis
segments.summary: He gives his name, says he was born in New Orleans in October 1938, and lived in Bay St. Louis, Mississippi from age 10 to 16.

segments.title: First hearing Papa Celestin's band around age 12
segments.summary: At about 12 he first heard Celestin's band at a yacht club; he and his friends loved it and went to all the dances to hear it.

segments.title: Parents' attitude and whether jazz was seen as art
segments.summary: His parents had known Dixieland since the 1920s and liked it without seeking it out; for his teenage group it was the only music, not thought of as art.

segments.title: Friends turn from Dixieland to rock and roll
segments.summary: He prefers more progressive music, while many friends switched to rock and roll after about 1953, though they have not wholly abandoned Dixieland.

segments.title: Good-time music or great music
segments.summary: He thinks most listeners treat New Orleans jazz as good-time dance music, like rhythm and blues, with a few appreciating it more deeply.

segments.title: Hiring Celestin for dances and debutante parties
segments.summary: From 1950 to 1953 everyone tried to book Celestin for social functions; today old bands are still hired, but debutant parties tend to get pop music.

segments.title: Closing remarks and thanks
segments.summary: Nothing more to add; thanks exchanged.
